anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata objects, forming blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, log, checkpoint, parallelism, and worker limits are mis-tuned so that the instance behaves far from the hardware or workload sweet spot.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream subscribers cannot receive, write, or apply primary WAL fast enough, causing widening lag and retention of old log segments.

When all three conditions coexist, the database experiences a compound failure pattern: lock waits and deadlocks inflate transaction runtimes, which in turn prolong WAL retention on the primary; mis-sized memory pools, lock-table limits, or checkpoint/replication parameters aggravate both the lock manager pressure and the replica’s ability to keep up; replication lag grows, consuming extra disk and amplifying checkpoint and flush bursts. Observable symptoms include exploding lock-wait time, deadlock-victim errors, plummeting TPS, surging WAL size on the primary, replay delay on replicas, uneven CPU and I/O utilization that does not match hardware capacity, and eventually application timeouts or failover unavailability.

Causally, sub-optimal configuration (e.g., small lock memory, aggressive lock-timeout, oversized checkpoints, too few replication sender/receiver buffers) reduces headroom in the lock manager and replication pipeline. Elevated lock contention keeps transactions open, preventing WAL recycling and forcing replicas to chase an ever-growing log backlog. The replica’s delayed apply can hold access-exclusive locks longer, feeding additional contention on the primary during logical decoding or cascading writes. Checkpoint storms triggered by mis-tuned parameters further spike I/O, lengthening both commit latency and replica catch-up time. The three anomalies therefore reinforce each other in a feedback loop that magnifies throughput collapse and durability risk.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
